label: meadow farmers, millers and bakers
identities: Farmers, millers and bakers who think most problems improve with a pie and a long talk.
Meadow folk who measure a year by its harvests and a neighbor by their bread.
architecture: Half-timbered cottages under deep thatch, round doors painted bright colors, and a windmill on every rise.
Stone bridges with a bench in the middle for talking, and barns big enough to hold a dance.

festivals.name: the Lantern Night
festivals.description: Every household hangs one lantern for each family member who traveled that year, and the whole valley glows.

festivals.name: the Hay Races
festivals.description: Hay-bale races, a tug-of-war across the millpond, and a pie judging that has ended friendships.

festivals.name: First Furrow
festivals.description: The oldest farmer cuts the first furrow while the children follow, planting wishes with the seed.

prides: No traveler has ever left one of their inns hungry.
Their first hearth has never once gone cold.

makersMarks: a wheat-ear stamped where the hand rests
a tiny pie burned or scratched somewhere hard to find
the maker's initials inside a lantern shape

moodLines: Ask the way in {adjective} country and you will be fed before you are answered.
Their villages smell of bread at dawn and woodsmoke at dusk.
Every quarrel here ends at the same long table.
Even their scarecrows look well looked after.
Some barns stand empty since the old roads closed, and someone still sweeps them.

label: woodwrights and grove-tenders
identities: Woodwrights and grove-tenders who share their villages with spirits.
Patient forest folk who grow their houses instead of building them.
architecture: Houses grown from living willow, rope bridges between great trees, and moth-lanterns on every branch.
Lacquered shrines among the roots and walkways that wind up the trunks.

festivals.name: Moth Lantern Night
festivals.description: Wish-carved lanterns float up into the canopy, and everyone pretends not to read their neighbors' wishes.

festivals.name: the Tending
festivals.description: The village asks the grove's patron spirit, very politely, how its year went.

festivals.name: First Leaf
festivals.description: The first leaf of the year is pressed into the village book, with a note on who spotted it.

prides: Their spirits trust them.
A grove they look after never goes wild.

makersMarks: a leaf carved so finely it seems to move
a drop of red lacquer shaped like a seed
the maker's grove-sign pressed in where the hand rests

moodLines: The {people} speak softly in the woods, because the woods are listening.
Every doorway has a little dish of water for whatever spirit is passing.
Their children learn the names of trees before the names of towns.
A {adjective} grove hums faintly on still evenings.
Some groves stopped answering long ago, and the {people} still leave them gifts.

label: terrace-builders, tea growers and bellfounders
identities: Terrace-builders, tea growers, bellfounders and kite-flyers.
Mountain folk who carved their fields into stairs and their stairs into poems.
architecture: Stepped stone terraces, curved tile roofs, and bells hung where the wind can ring them.
Bridges strung from peak to peak, with a tea house at each end.

festivals.name: Kite Day
festivals.description: Every family flies a kite with its wishes painted on, and the highest kite's wish is read aloud.

festivals.name: the Ringing
festivals.description: Every bell in the valley rings once at dawn, in order, from the highest terrace down.

festivals.name: First Pick
festivals.description: The first tea leaves are picked by the youngest and brewed for the oldest.

values: climbing a little higher each year
prides: Their bridges have stood for centuries, and they will mention this.
Their bells can be heard three valleys away.

makersMarks: a tiny bell engraved where the hand rests
the number of steps from the maker's door, in small careful script
a kite-shaped seal in red wax

moodLines: In {adjective} country the bells keep time and the kites keep score.
Tea is served on every landing, and every landing has a view.
The {people} climb slowly and arrive first.
Each terrace step is signed by the family who laid it.
A few high bells have hung silent for generations, and nobody will melt them down.

label: sunny harbor folk and lighthouse keepers
identities: Sunny harbor folk who keep the lighthouses lit.
Sailors, net-makers and lens-grinders who would rather be at sea and usually are.
architecture: White-walled houses stacked up the cliffs, blue shutters, and a lighthouse on every point.
Quays wide enough for a market, and a bell for every boat still out.

festivals.name: the Regatta
festivals.description: Every boat that floats races around the point, and a few that don't race anyway.

festivals.name: Lamp-Lighting at the Point
festivals.description: The lighthouse keepers walk the cliff path with torches and the whole town follows them.

festivals.name: the Blessing of the Nets
festivals.description: Nets are spread across the square and children run under them for luck.

values: never turning a stranger away from the quay
prides: Their lighthouses have never all gone dark at once.
Their sailors have reached shores nobody else has drawn.

makersMarks: a tiny lighthouse etched where the hand rests
a knot of blue thread wound somewhere snug
the maker's ship-name stamped backward, for luck

moodLines: The {people} talk with their hands, mostly about boats.
Every harbor wall is warm by noon and crowded by evening.
A {adjective} welcome comes with a bowl of stew and too many questions.
They paint their doors the color of the sea on a good day.
Some lamps on the point are still lit for boats that never came back.

label: mesa potters, glassblowers and star-readers
identities: Mesa potters, glassblowers and star-readers who run the great caravans.
Red-country folk who read the sky like a ledger and the desert like a friend.
architecture: Cliff houses of red clay, cool courtyards with a well at the center, and kilns that glow all night.
Caravan halls with sun-clocks on every wall and star charts painted on the ceilings.

festivals.name: the Night of Counting
festivals.description: Everyone lies on the warm rooftops and counts falling stars until the youngest falls asleep.

festivals.name: Caravan Return
festivals.description: The great caravans come home, and every family sets a place for a traveler they haven't met.

festivals.name: the First Firing
festivals.description: The kilns are lit together, and the first pot out is given away.

prides: Their caravans have never lost a well.
Their glass holds the noon light longer than anyone's.

makersMarks: a thumbprint pressed in somewhere it will last
a small star etched where the light catches
a knot pattern unique to the maker's caravan

moodLines: The {people} bargain like it is a dance, and it is.
Their courtyards are cool at noon and full of music at night.
Every guest gets the last fig, and every guest knows it.
A {adjective} star chart is a family heirloom and a running argument.
Some wells along the old routes have dried, and the {people} still mark them on every map.

label: northern herders and storytellers
identities: Northern herders and storytellers who measure winters in tales.
Snow-country folk who keep the fire high and the stories longer.
architecture: Long turf-roofed halls with a fire down the middle, and carved posts telling the family's stories.
Snug lodges half under the snow, joined by roofed walkways.

festivals.name: Sun-Return
festivals.description: The whole village climbs the ridge to cheer the first sunrise after the long dark.

festivals.name: the Long Telling
festivals.description: One story is told across a whole week of nights, and nobody is allowed to guess the ending.

festivals.name: the Herd-Coming
festivals.description: The herds come down from the high pastures and every bell on every collar rings at once.

values: sharing the warm spot by the fire
prides: No guest has ever been turned out into the snow.
Their stories outlast their halls.

makersMarks: a knot carved in where the hand rests
a tally of winters notched along one edge
a twist of red wool tied through a hole made for it

moodLines: Winters are long in {adjective} country, so the stories are longer.
Every hall keeps one seat by the fire for whoever walks in next.
The {people} laugh loudest in the coldest weeks.
Their herds know the way home better than most maps.
Some halls stand roofless on the old ridges, and travelers still knock before entering.

label: stilt-village ferry-keepers
identities: Stilt-village ferry-keepers famous for frog choirs and terrible puns.
Fen folk who know every channel, every eel and every joke worth telling twice.
architecture: Stilt houses joined by plank walks, reed roofs, and a ferry bell at every landing.
Floating gardens tied to the porches and lanterns hung low over the water.

festivals.name: the Frog Choir
festivals.description: The whole village sings with the frogs at dusk, and judges say the frogs win every year.

festivals.name: Big-Dry Day
festivals.description: When the water is lowest, everyone walks the fen floor to find what the year has dropped.

festivals.name: Lantern Float
festivals.description: Gourd lanterns are floated down every channel to show the ferries the way home.

values: never laughing at a joke too early
prides: Their ferries have never once refused a passenger.
Their puns are, by common agreement, the worst anywhere.

makersMarks: a little frog carved somewhere hard to find
three dots of green paint
a reed knot only the maker can tie

moodLines: The {people} answer every question with a pun and then, kindly, with the answer.
Mornings in the fens are foggy, slow and full of frog song.
A {adjective} ferry will wait for you, and tease you the whole way across.
Their gardens float, and so, they claim, do their spirits.
Some channels silted up long ago, and the {people} still pole past them quietly.

label: smiths, miners and clockmakers
identities: Smiths, miners and clockmakers who can fix anything and will tell you how.
Hill folk who sing while they hammer and hammer while they sing.
architecture: Workshops dug into the hillside, with chimneys poking out of the grass like mushrooms.
Arched halls lit by forge-glow, with a clock over every door.

festivals.name: the Anvil Chorus
festivals.description: Every smith strikes the same rhythm at the same hour, and the whole hill rings.

festivals.name: Clock-Winding Day
festivals.description: Every clock in town is wound together, and anyone whose clock is late buys the next round.

festivals.name: the Open Forge
festivals.description: Workshops open to everyone, and children make their first nail.

prides: Their clocks agree with each other to the second.
A hinge they made has never squeaked.

makersMarks: a tiny hammer stamped where the hand rests
the maker's number struck small and neat
a single notch filed where only another smith would look

moodLines: The {people} greet you with a handshake that checks your grip.
Their hills ring all day and glow all night.
A {adjective} smith will fix your kettle and lecture you about it, kindly.
Every tool has a name and a story, and both are long.
Some deep workings were sealed long ago, and the {people} still knock twice when they pass.

label: orchard-keepers, beekeepers and cider-makers
identities: Orchard-keepers, beekeepers and cider-makers who plant trees for grandchildren they haven't met.
Valley folk who run their lives by the blossom and the harvest.
architecture: Cottages tucked between the rows, with skeps along every wall and a press-house at the heart of the village.
Long low barns that smell of apples all year.

festivals.name: Blossom Day
festivals.description: Everyone walks the rows under the blossom, and the bees are thanked by name.

festivals.name: the Wassail
festivals.description: The oldest tree in the orchard is sung to, toasted, and told it is doing very well.

festivals.name: the Pressing
festivals.description: The first barrel of the year is opened, and arguments about it last until spring.

prides: Their oldest tree still fruits every year.
Nobody leaves their valley without a basket.

makersMarks: a tiny bee pressed in where the hand rests
a blossom stamped somewhere it will catch the light
the year's vintage scratched small and neat

moodLines: The {people} measure time in blossoms and harvests, never in hours.
Their valleys hum with bees from spring to first frost.
A {adjective} cider is shared, argued over, and shared again.
Every child plants a tree and is told it will outlive them, cheerfully.
Some old orchards stand unpicked, and the {people} still prune them every winter.

label: herders, riders and kite-flyers of the open plains
identities: Herders and riders who follow the wind and their herds across the open plains.
Plains folk who can read weather from a single cloud.
architecture: Round felt tents that come down in an hour and go up in two.
Painted wind-poles at every camp, hung with bells and ribbons.

festivals.name: the Long Ride
festivals.description: Riders race from one camp to the next, and the winner must cook for everyone.

festivals.name: Kite Night
festivals.description: Lantern-kites are flown over the plain so that far-off camps can wave back.

festivals.name: the Gathering
festivals.description: Every camp meets at the same river bend to trade, marry and tell tall tales.

prides: They have never been lost on the plains.
Their kites can carry a letter between camps.

makersMarks: a hoofprint stamped where the hand rests
a ribbon of the maker's camp colors
a little cloud scratched where only a rider would look

moodLines: The {people} never say goodbye, only see you at the Gathering.
Their camps move with the grass and leave nothing but circles of greener ground.
A {adjective} rider can tell tomorrow's weather from today's breeze.
Every tent has a guest-cushion that nobody else may sit on.
Some old camp-circles are still green, and the {people} ride around them, never through.
